As of 17 June 2026, authorities have recorded more than 100 deaths and hundreds of confirmed infections caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which there is no licensed vaccine. In sixteen previous outbreaks, the responsible virus was Zaire ebolavirus, a strain health authorities have been able to contain more effectively. The current outbreak in Ituri underscores challenges posed by Bundibugyo ebolavirus and complicates control efforts in the conflict-affected east. Separately, Kinshasa faces controversy over participating in a U.S.-led program to deport illegal migrants to third countries, including the reception of 15 Latin American nationals.

articleSummary: As of 17 June 2026, seven people cured of Ebola virus disease have left the Rwampara Ebola Treatment Center at the General Reference Hospital of Rwampara in Ituri, Democratic Republic of the Congo, including the first baby officially cured in this outbreak after 17 days of treatment. The seven survivors comprise one infant, four women and two men. Health officials note that nine people have been officially declared cured and allowed to return home since the outbreak began in the area, while about twenty suspected cases tested negative and were discharged. Ituri remains the epicenter of the Ebola outbreak in the DRC. Authorities stress that early treatment at a dedicated center greatly improves survival and urge communities to seek care promptly, aiming to counter rumors and stigma while strengthening prevention efforts.

articleSummary: UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said escalating violence in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to exact a heavy toll on civilians, hampering relief efforts and jeopardizing containment of the Ebola outbreak. In North Kivu, fighting in Walikale and Masisi forced hundreds of families to flee; on June 13, shelling of Munda and Bohimba killed at least three civilians and wounded five, with health facilities and schools shut because of the violence. In South Kivu, aid workers report ongoing hostilities including airstrikes, shelling, and gunfire in populated areas. These actions further disrupt humanitarian access, leaving more people without aid and elevating the risk of Ebola transmission as people move between affected provinces. Displacement and movement raise concerns for outbreak control.

articleSummary: KAP assessment of Ebola virus disease outbreak (June 2026) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Ituri, eastern DRC) following the May 15, 2026 declaration of a Bundibugyo-strain outbreak—the 17th in the country since 1976—with no approved vaccine or specific treatment. articleSummary: Beijing’s Chaoyang Hospital head Li Haichao warns that summer respiratory infections are common, dominated by upper infections caused by rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and adenovirus. Air conditioning should not be set too cold, and regular ventilation and AC maintenance are important to reduce risks of Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia. Cough can persist 3–8 weeks; if no significant improvement after two weeks, evaluate for other causes. articleSummary: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) is rising in Ho Chi Minh City and southern Vietnam. In Week 23 (June 1–7, 2026), the city reported 1,160 HFMD cases, up 13.3% from the four-week average; cumulative 20,406 cases since the start of 2026. A severe case involved a 10-year-old girl from Tan My ward presenting on day 5 with fever to 40°C, vesicles on hands, feet, knees, and elbows, and neurological signs. She was diagnosed HFMD grade 3 with brainstem injury on MRI, metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, and mild liver enzyme rise. articleHeadline: Africa's Ebola outbreaks complicated by victims who prefer traditional healers over hospitals
articleSummary: Ebola in Congo’s Ituri region, centered on Bunia, is driven by the Bundibugyo virus—the rare Ebola type with no approved medicines or vaccines—killing at least 181 people as the outbreak unfolds. articleHeadline: WHO issues comprehensive guidelines on filovirus disease, including Ebola and Marburg disease
articleSummary: WHO released its first guidelines for clinical management of filovirus disease—covering all Ebola and Marburg viruses—in response to the Democratic Republic of the Congo's Bundibugyo virus Ebola outbreak. The guidelines emphasize early supportive care and present 16 evidence-based recommendations. Filovirus diseases have case fatality rates ranging from 25% to 90% in severe outbreaks; since 1967 there have been 72 outbreaks in Africa. With no licensed vaccines or treatments for Marburg virus disease, Bundibugyo- and Sudan virus diseases rely on early supportive care to improve survival. Key recommendations include prioritized laboratory tests to monitor for hypoglycemia and metabolic disturbances; rapid rehydration (oral/IV); early use of IV fluids and vasopressors guided by vitals and perfusion; treatment of bacterial co-infections with antibiotics; and structured after-care for survivors to reduce viral persistence risks. For Bundibugyo virus disease, early recognition, rapid referral, and optimized supportive care remain essential; guidelines aim to harmonize care and preparedness.

articleHeadline: WHO Releases Guidelines on Ebola, Marburg Disease
articleSummary: DRC is contending with an Ebola outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus as WHO releases its first comprehensive clinical management guidelines for filovirus diseases, encompassing all Ebola and Marburg types. Published 2026-06-17, the guidance emphasizes early supportive care and presents 16 evidence-based recommendations to improve survival, monitor deterioration, manage dehydration, and support post-recovery follow-up. Ebola and Marburg outbreaks can yield case fatality rates from 25% to 90%; Africa has recorded 72 outbreaks since Marburg’s 1967 discovery. With no licensed vaccines or treatments for Marburg, Bundibugyo and Sudan virus diseases, optimized supportive care is foundational and enables antiviral research. For Bundibugyo virus disease, early recognition, rapid referral, and precise supportive therapies are fundamental. Recommendations include prioritized laboratory tests for hypoglycemia and metabolic issues, rapid rehydration (oral/IV), cautious use of IV fluids and vasoactive meds for shock with serial monitoring, and treating bacterial co-infections when present to ensure safe survivorship care.

articleSummary: International concern mounts over Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with confirmed cases reported across multiple regions more than a month after official announcements. Exact case counts remain unclear as the outbreak expands, hindered by severe logistical challenges, a shortage of specialized treatment centers, and deteriorating medical infrastructure to accommodate rising patient numbers in provincial areas. Widespread international anxiety is fueled by resistance from some communities to strict health measures aimed at limiting transmission in remote, densely populated zones. The true scale of the crisis is unknown due to data gaps, complicating rapid response and precise mapping of spread, and raising the risk of a large humanitarian catastrophe if coordination remains weak. Experts advocate intensified community outreach and engagement of local leaders to secure public cooperation with medical teams and enable early detection of suspected cases before they seed further clusters.

The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo strain, with a 30–50% fatality rate and no approved vaccine or specific treatment. Transmission is via direct contact with bodily fluids, causing hemorrhagic fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and internal bleeding. Uganda is affected alongside the DRC. Public health measures face funding and logistics challenges that impede containment.

articleHeadline: Why are experts warning latest Ebola outbreak could be 'worst ever'?
articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri; North and South Kivu) is driven by Bundibugyo virus, with 837 cases and 196 deaths in DRC and 19 cases with 2 deaths in Uganda. articleSummary: The Ebola outbreak declared an international health emergency by WHO risks becoming the worst in history, according to Africa CDC Director Jean Kaseya. articleHeadline: New evidence of origin of the black death a 'complete surprise' experts say
articleSummary: Ancient DNA from 46 Lake Baikal hunter-gatherer burials (ca. 5,500 years ago) revealed Yersinia pestis in 18 individuals, indicating a large-scale plague outbreak long before medieval pandemics. Findings, published in Nature on 2026-06-17, show the pathogen killed many youths among the buried, with genetics in these ancient strains linked to high virulence for children. The prehistoric plague lacked a gene needed for efficient flea-borne transmission but carried a variant absent in later strains that can cause inflammatory complications. Researchers propose marmots as the original host and place the origin of plague in central/northeastern Asia before its spread across Eurasia, challenging the view that farming and cities were the sole drivers. In modern times, plague remains a few hundred cases annually worldwide and is curable with antibiotics.

articleHeadline: Alerta na dengue: Idosos concentram 42% dos casos graves em Uberaba
articleSummary: Dengue disproportionately affects the elderly in Uberaba, Brazil: individuals aged 60+ accounted for 42% of severe dengue cases, despite representing only 14% of dengue notifications nationwide. In a retrospective study of 55 seniors treated at Hospital de Clínicas da Universidade Federal do Triângulo Mineiro from 2014–2024, researchers assessed clinical features, comorbidities, and disease progression. Findings: 83.63% had at least one comorbidity; 53.2% exhibited severe thrombocytopenia; hepatic alterations and greater clinical vulnerability were observed as infection evolved. Authors warn that aging can mask typical dengue manifestations, leading to delayed clinical recognition, especially during periods of high transmission. They advocate revising international protocols to include geriatric-specific criteria to improve early identification of those at greater risk. No vaccine currently approved for all elderly profiles; emphasis on clinical monitoring and early signs. Plans for expanded research and potential public health policy implications.

articleHeadline: WHO launches landmark guidelines to combat Ebola and Marburg threats
articleSummary: WHO released its first unified clinical guidelines for Ebola and Marburg virus diseases, comprising 16 evidence-based recommendations to reduce deaths and strengthen outbreak response. The framework covers all Ebola virus species and Marburg virus disease, providing a single, standardized approach for frontline clinicians and policymakers. The guidelines arrive as the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) confronts a fresh Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo strain, underscoring the need for cohesive management. Developed through global expert consultation and current evidence, they emphasize early supportive care, rapid rehydration (oral and IV), treatment of shock, close monitoring and swift handling of complications. They advise early laboratory testing to treat reversible conditions like hypoglycaemia, and prompt antibiotics when bacterial infections or sepsis are suspected. The package also prioritizes early deterioration detection, survival follow-up for viral persistence, and integration into national plans to bolster preparedness.

articleSummary: Ebola is transmitted primarily through contact with infected animals or their bodily fluids, and through contact with an infected person; it is not spread through the air like influenza or COVID-19. Outbreaks have raised global concern, notably in Congo and Uganda, amplified by modern travel. Typical onset includes high fever, severe fatigue, weakness, muscle and throat pains; as illness progresses, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rash may occur, with kidney and liver dysfunction potentially developing. In severe cases, internal and external bleeding can occur, with blood appearing in vomit or stool, and sometimes from the nose, mouth, gums, or vagina. Some survivors experience long-term effects such as persistent fatigue, headaches, muscle and joint pain, vision problems, eye pain, light sensitivity, abdominal pain, and loss of appetite.
